:::{#def-expectation}
#### Expectation, expected value, population mean

The **expectation**, **expected value**, or **population mean** of a
*discrete* random variable $X$, denoted $\E{X}$, $\mu(X)$, or $\mu_X$,
is the mean of $X$'s possible values,
weighted by the [probability mass function](random-variables.qmd#def-pmf) of those values:

$$\E{X} \eqdef \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} x \cdot \P(X=x)$$

The **expectation** of a *continuous* random variable $X$
with [probability density function](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) $\p(X=x)$
is the mean of $X$'s possible values, weighted by that density:

$$\E{X} \eqdef \int_{x\in \rangef{X}} x \cdot \p(X=x)\,dx$$

In both cases, the expectation is defined
only when the sum or integral converges absolutely,
that is, when it is finite with $\abs{x}$ in place of $x$.

:::

::: notes

A random variable whose expectation is not defined is not exotic:
a random variable with density $\p(X=x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)}$
(the standard Cauchy distribution) has none,
because $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \abs{x} \cd \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)}\,dx$ diverges.

See also <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_value>

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-bernoulli-mean}
#### Expectation of the Bernoulli distribution

If $X \sim \Ber(\pi)$, that is, $\P(X = 1) = \pi$ and $\P(X = 0) = 1 - \pi$, then:

$$\E{X} = \pi$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

$$
\ba
\E{X}
&= \sum_{x\in \rangef{X}} x \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(definition of expectation for discrete r.v.)}
\\&= \sum_{x\in \set{0,1}} x \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(range of Bernoulli r.v. is } \{0, 1\} \text{)}
\\&= \paren{0 \cd \P(X=0)} + \paren{1 \cd \P(X=1)} && \text{(expand sum over } x = 0 \text{ and } x = 1 \text{)}
\\&= \paren{0 \cd (1-\pi)} + \paren{1 \cd \pi} && \text{(substitute Bernoulli PMF values)}
\\&= 0 + \pi && \text{(multiplication by 0 and 1)}
\\&= \pi && \text{(addition of 0)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-surv-mean}
#### Expectation of time-to-event variables

If $T$ is a non-negative random variable
with [survival function](random-variables.qmd#def-surv-fn) $\surv(t)$, then:

$$\E{T} = \int_{t=0}^{\infty} \surv(t)\,dt$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

<!-- The Fubini-Tonelli link points at rme until mds's multi-page site is published; repoint it to mds's calculus page (calculus.html#thm-fubini-tonelli) then. -->

We prove the continuous case, in which $T$ has a density $\pdf$.
The integrand $\pdf(u) \cd \indicp{0 \le t \le u}$ is non-negative
on $[0, \infty) \times [0, \infty)$,
so Tonelli's theorem
(the non-negative case of the
[Fubini--Tonelli theorem](https://morrison-lab.github.io/rme/chapters/math-prereqs.html#thm-fubini-tonelli);
@billingsley1995probability, Theorem 18.3)
lets us exchange the order of integration:

$$
\ba
\E{T}
&= \int_{u=0}^{\infty} u\,\pdf(u)\,du
&& \text{(definition of expectation; } T \ge 0 \text{)}\\
&= \int_{u=0}^{\infty}\paren{\int_{t=0}^{u} 1\,dt}\pdf(u)\,du
&& \text{(} u = \textstyle\int_0^u 1\,dt \text{)}\\
&= \int_{u=0}^{\infty}\int_{t=0}^{u} \pdf(u)\,dt\,du
&& \text{(move } \pdf(u) \text{ inside the inner integral)}\\
&= \int_{t=0}^{\infty}\int_{u=t}^{\infty} \pdf(u)\,du\,dt
&& \text{(Tonelli: exchange the order over } 0 \le t \le u \text{)}\\
&= \int_{t=0}^{\infty}\Pr(T>t)\,dt
&& \text{(integrate the density over } (t, \infty) \text{)}\\
&= \int_{t=0}^{\infty}\surv(t)\,dt
&& \text{(definition of the survival function)}
\ea
$$

See [@statproofbook:mean-nnrvar] for an alternative presentation of this proof.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-fubini-survfn}

#### Mean of an exponential random variable via survival function

Let $T$ be exponential with rate $\lambda > 0$, so $\surv(t) = \ef{-\lambda t}$
for $t \ge 0$,
as computed on the [random variables page](random-variables.qmd#exm-exp-survfn).
By @thm-surv-mean:

$$
\ba
\E{T}
&= \int_0^\infty \surv(t)\,dt
&& \text{(expectation via the survival function)}\\
&= \int_0^\infty \ef{-\lambda t}\,dt
&& \text{(substitute the survival function)}\\
&= \sb{-\frac{1}{\lambda}\ef{-\lambda t}}_0^\infty
&& \text{(antiderivative)}\\
&= 0 - \paren{-\frac{1}{\lambda}}
&& \text{(evaluate at the bounds)}\\
&= \frac{1}{\lambda}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-expectation-matrix}

#### Expectation of a random matrix

For a random matrix $\matr{A}$ of size $m \times n$
with $(i,j)$-th element $A_{ij}$,
the **expectation** $\Expp\matr{A}$ is the $m \times n$ matrix
whose $(i,j)$-th element is $\E{A_{ij}}$:

$$
\Expp\matr{A} \eqdef \pmat{
  \E{A_{11}} & \E{A_{12}} & \cdots & \E{A_{1n}} \\
  \E{A_{21}} & \E{A_{22}} & \cdots & \E{A_{2n}} \\
  \vdots     & \vdots     & \ddots & \vdots     \\
  \E{A_{m1}} & \E{A_{m2}} & \cdots & \E{A_{mn}}
}
$$

:::

::: notes

In other words, expectation is applied **element-wise** to a random matrix.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-expectation-matrix}
#### Expectation of a random vector of coin flips

For the two fair coin flips in [the independence page's example](independence.qmd#exm-indpt),
the random vector $\vX = \tp{(X_1, X_2)}$ is a $2 \times 1$ random matrix, and:

$$\Expp\vX = \pmat{\E{X_1} \\ \E{X_2}} = \pmat{1/2 \\ 1/2}$$

since each $X_i$ is Bernoulli with $\pi = 1/2$ (@thm-bernoulli-mean).

:::
